entry.evidence: The main contribution of this work is to use and develop new statistical machine-learning methods for the seismic event classification problem.

steps.action: The study takes the existing Åknes geophone event database: 16 s windows from 8 three-component geophones, triggered by an amplitude threshold and labelled by experts into eight classes, plus 1611 unlabelled 2021 events.
steps.quote: Based on expert opinion, every event is then labeled into one of eight classes, as described in Table 1.

steps.action: The authors describe how the classes differ in spectrograms (duration, envelope shape, frequency content) and how records vary between sensors for the same event.
steps.quote: There are apparent differences in the signals.

steps.action: The authors ask how all 24 time series per event can be used to improve classification.
steps.quote: a natural question is then ’how one can use all this information?’

steps.action: The authors state two assumptions behind ensemble prediction: each time series carries enough information alone, and aggregating the spectrograms weakens useful information. These set ensemble prediction against early aggregation.
steps.quote: If spectrograms of the 24 time series are aggregated, useful information on some of the 24 spectrograms might be weakened.

steps.action: The authors build the ensemble prediction (Algorithm 1): during training a random single-channel spectrogram is drawn per event; at test time the softmax outputs of all 24 channels are averaged.
steps.quote: Pseudocode for the ensemble prediction is presented in Algorithm 1.

steps.action: The authors propose that representations must encode temporal transitions, which VIbCReg lacks.
steps.quote: The necessity of encoding the temporal transition can be observed given several samples from our dataset in Fig. 2.

steps.action: The authors build VNIbCReg, a self-supervised method that combines VIbCReg with TNC, adds a correlation term to the TNC loss and adds sensor invariance across the 24 channels; λ, μ, ν are taken from earlier work and ρ is set by grid search.
steps.quote: TNC is adopted into VIbCReg, resulting in VNIbCReg

steps.action: The authors design the experiments: stratified 80/20 split, three seeds, SciPy spectrograms (0.08 s window, single channel, rectangular), weighted SNR aggregation for the non-ensemble case, AlexNet versus ResNet34, Adam optimizer, accuracy and confusion matrices. They report that the Langet and Silverberg preprocessing overfit in their runs.
steps.quote: the dataset is split by stratified random sampling into 80% for training and 20% for testing

steps.action: On aggregated spectrograms, the authors compare AlexNet with ResNet34, with and without class weights (Table 2: about 0.87 versus 0.88), and adopt class weights from then on.
steps.quote: Table 2 shows that ResNet outperforms AlexNet in terms of accuracy

steps.action: The authors compare ensemble prediction with aggregated spectrograms (Table 3): ResNet34 rises from 0.878 to 0.928 and AlexNet from 0.867 to 0.916. Confusion matrices (Fig. 12) and per-channel examples (Fig. 13) are shown.
steps.quote: ResNet34 with the ensemble prediction performs the best in terms of accuracy.

steps.action: The authors check that the ensemble gain holds across the two architectures.
steps.quote: The noticeable test accuracy improvement compared with Table 2 is seen for both [...] .

steps.action: The authors design an ablation over intermediate variants between VIbCReg and VNIbCReg (random versus neighboring crop, original versus modified TNC loss), with a randomly initialised encoder as baseline.
steps.quote: The evaluation on the intermediate variants is conducted to find out how much contribution each component that is added on VIbCReg to form VNIbCReg makes.

steps.action: In linear evaluation (Table 4), the authors compare SSL encoders with RandInit (0.642): TNC scores 0.499, VIbCReg 0.476 and VNIbCReg 0.716.
steps.quote: VIbCReg does not perform so well here

steps.action: Ablation result: adding neighboring crop and the TNC loss raises linear accuracy step by step, and the modified loss raises it further.
steps.quote: a significant improvement is achieved in the linear evaluation

steps.action: In fine-tuning evaluation (Table 5) on 5%, 10% and 80% of the labels, VNIbCReg is best with few labels (0.717 and 0.824 versus RandInit 0.185 and 0.528). RandInit is best at 80% (0.928).
steps.quote: VNIbCReg results in the highest test accuracy in the small dataset regime

steps.action: The authors check that the method ranking is the same under the two evaluation protocols (linear and fine-tuning) and across label fractions.
steps.quote: The performance ranking order of the fine-tuning evaluation between VIbCReg, VNIbCReg, and the intermediate variants remains the same as in the linear evaluation.

steps.action: The authors reject early aggregation of the 24 channels as the default practice.
steps.quote: early aggregation to improve the signal-to-noise ratio is not necessarily beneficial

steps.action: The authors keep two claims: ensemble prediction gives substantial accuracy gains, and SSL pretraining helps when labels are scarce.
steps.quote: Self-supervised learning methods also gave good performance for our case, particularly so when labeled training data lacks.

tree.answer: Distinct classes of microseismic events at the Åknes rock slope, already labelled by experts
Yes; recorded by geophones, but class labels come from expert judgement
A better automatic classifier (a method), not a geophysical claim
Methods compete: aggregation versus ensemble, AlexNet versus ResNet34, SSL variants versus random initialisation
No quantitative predictions stated beforehand; rivals are ranked by held-out test accuracy
Conditions set computationally: splits, architectures, augmentations, label fractions
Partly: three seeds, two architectures, two evaluation protocols, three label fractions; no independent data
Ensemble prediction kept; VNIbCReg kept for small labelled sets

end.claim: Ensemble prediction over the 24 single-channel spectrograms raises held-out accuracy on the eight-class Åknes dataset from 0.878 to 0.928 (ResNet34) and from 0.867 to 0.916 (AlexNet), compared with aggregated spectrograms.

decisive_move.sentence: The ensemble-versus-aggregation comparison on held-out data (Table 3) is the step without which the headline claim would not exist.

gates.evidence: The data and labels were collected by routine threshold-triggered monitoring before this study (§2 ¶5), so no hypothesis directed acquisition. The ensemble and SSL claims faced held-out test comparisons that could have shown no gain (Tables 3–5), but no threshold or analysis plan was fixed in advance. ρ was set by grid search and the preprocessing was chosen after seeing lower accuracy with the alternative (§5 ¶8, §6.1 ¶3); the paper does not say whether this tuning used the test split.

imports.item: Linear and fine-tuning evaluation protocols for SSL

novelty_claims.quote: VNIbCReg is an SSL method proposed for the event classification in this paper.
Ensemble prediction substantially improves on the state-of-the-art classification for this Åknes case study.
denotes the modified TNC loss proposed in this work.

limits: Labels are expert judgements, which the authors say are not ground truth (§2 ¶5). Data availability mentions a cross-check against the NORSAR bulletin (p. 397), but no inter-rater agreement is reported. All tests use random splits of one site's archive; there is no held-out time period or other site, and the generalisation to reservoirs and DAS data (§7 ¶3) is asserted, not tested. Uncertainty is three seeds without significance tests. The AlexNet–ResNet gap (0.867 vs 0.878) lies within about one standard deviation (Table 2). Sub-claim: VNIbCReg pretraining improves accuracy with 5–10% of the labels (capability_characterized, Table 5). At 80% labels, however, RandInit (0.928) beats every SSL variant, so SSL gives no gain with full labels. Inference: the paper does not state whether SSL fine-tuning used ensemble prediction. Inference: hyperparameter and preprocessing choices may have been made on test performance; the paper is silent on a validation split. Step 1 is coded inherited because co-author Langet produced the labelled database (Langet and Silverberg 2022); this is an inference. Composition none_fits: the walk is method benchmarking (new methods, then compared against baselines on a fixed labelled archive), which matches none of the listed compositions. No review file was supplied.

disagreements.target: Langet and Silverberg (2022) spectrogram preprocessing (1 s window, 95% overlap, 3×224×224 RGB)
disagreements.support: The authors report that this preprocessing overfit and gave lower accuracy in their experiments, and argue that squishing spectrograms into square RGB images loses information; no table of these runs is shown.
disagreements.quote: The sliding window length and overlap give monotonous spectrograms i.e. low-resolution spectrogram, and it leads to an overfitting which give lower accuracy in our experiments.

disagreements.target: Early-averaging approaches in signal processing (Ovanger 2021; Langet and Silverberg 2022)
disagreements.support: Ensemble prediction without pre-aggregation beats aggregated spectrograms by about 5 accuracy points for both architectures (Table 3).
disagreements.quote: The lesson learned from this is that early aggregation to improve the signal-to-noise ratio is not necessarily beneficial.

disagreements.target: AlexNet as the standard CNN in previous Åknes studies (Langet and Silverberg 2022)
disagreements.support: ResNet34 scores slightly higher than AlexNet with about a third of the parameters (Tables 2–3).
disagreements.quote: Table 2 shows that ResNet outperforms AlexNet in terms of accuracy

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Aligning and aggregating the time series into one average spectrogram per event
alternatives_considered.reason: No information loss from pre-aggregation; better uncertainty assessment
Representation size of 512 as in VIbCReg; larger capacity than ResNet18; three times fewer parameters than AlexNet

alternatives_considered.reason: Improves representation quality by correlating neighbours and decorrelating non-neighbours

alternatives_considered.reason: Suggested values from earlier work; grid search
